course: Daily Pig Sales: Batch Farrowing System
module_title: Selling Every Day: Marketing and Buyers

lessons.title: Butchers vs Live Traders
lessons.body: When you sell pigs daily, you have two main buyer types: butchers and live traders. A butcher buys slaughtered carcasses or live pigs to slaughter and sell as meat. A live trader buys live pigs to resell, often at markets or to other farmers. Each has different needs and payment terms. Butchers want consistent weight and quality. They pay per kilogram of carcass or live weight. In many African markets, a butcher might pay 2,500 to 3,500 shillings per kg of carcass, depending on the country and season. They prefer pigs weighing 80-100 kg live, yielding about 70-75% carcass. Live traders often pay less per kg because they need a margin for transport and resale. They may pay 1,800 to 2,500 shillings per kg live weight. But they buy in bulk and pay cash quickly. Your choice depends on your volume and location. If you are near a town with butcheries, focus on butchers. If you are remote, live traders may be your only option. Butchers demand regular supplyâif you promise 5 pigs every Monday, you must deliver. Live traders are more flexible but less reliable. Start by visiting local butcheries and market stalls. Ask about their weekly needs, prices, and payment terms. Keep a notebook of each buyer's requirements. For daily sales from batch farrowing, you need at least 3-4 regular buyers to avoid dependence on one. Mix butchers and live traders to balance price and reliability. Remember, a live trader might pay cash today but disappear tomorrow. A butcher may pay later but buys every week. Build relationships slowly. Offer consistent quality, and you can negotiate better prices.

lessons.title: Contract With a Butcher
lessons.body: A contract with a butcher protects you from price drops and guarantees a market. It does not need to be a legal documentâa simple written agreement signed by both parties works in most African settings. Include these key points: number of pigs per week, weight range (e.g., 80-90 kg live), price per kg (or a formula based on market price), payment terms (cash on delivery or within 7 days), and penalties for missed deliveries. For example, you agree to supply 4 pigs every Tuesday. The butcher agrees to pay 2,800 shillings per kg live weight, with a 5% bonus if you deliver before 9 AM. If you miss a delivery without notice, you pay a penalty of 10% of the value. If the butcher fails to pay within 7 days, you charge 2% interest per week. Both parties should keep a copy. In practice, many butchers prefer verbal agreements, but a written contract reduces disputes. Start with a 3-month trial. Review after 3 months and adjust prices based on feed costs and market trends. For daily sales from batch farrowing, a contract ensures you can plan your batches. You know exactly how many pigs you need each week. That helps you schedule farrowing and weaning. Without a contract, you might have pigs ready but no buyer. With a contract, you can invest in better feed and health care. Some butchers will also pay a deposit upfrontâuse that to buy feed. Always deliver on time and at the agreed weight. If your pigs are underweight, the butcher may reject them or pay less. Weigh your pigs before delivery. Use a weighing crate or a scale. If you don't have a scale, use a weigh tape. Consistency builds trust. After 6 months, you can negotiate a higher price or a longer contract. A good butcher relationship can last years.

lessons.title: Pricing to Protect Margin
lessons.body: Your selling price must cover feed, labor, health, and transport, and still leave a profit. Many pig farmers fail because they price based on what buyers offer, not on their costs. Calculate your cost per kg of live weight. Start with feedâit is 60-70% of costs. A pig eats about 250 kg of feed from weaning to 90 kg live weight. If feed costs 1,200 shillings per 50 kg bag, that is 24 shillings per kg of feed. So feed cost per pig = 250 kg x 24 = 6,000 shillings. Add health (vaccines, dewormers) at 500 shillings, labor at 1,000 shillings, and transport at 500 shillings. Total cost = 8,000 shillings. If the pig weighs 90 kg live, your cost per kg = 8,000 / 90 = 89 shillings per kg. But that is only costâyou need profit. A 30% margin means you sell at 89 x 1.3 = 116 shillings per kg. However, market prices in many African countries range from 1,800 to 3,500 shillings per kg live weight. Waitâthat is per kg of carcass? No, live weight prices are often 1,500 to 2,500 shillings per kg in local currency. Check your local market. The key is to know your cost and set a floor price. Never sell below cost. If a live trader offers 1,200 shillings per kg and your cost is 1,500, you lose money. Instead, find a butcher who pays 2,000. Also consider weight: heavier pigs have lower cost per kg because feed efficiency improves. But too heavy (over 110 kg) may be rejected. Aim for 80-100 kg. Track every sale in a notebook: date, buyer, weight, price, and costs. After one month, calculate your average margin. If margin is below 20%, raise prices or cut feed costs by mixing your own rations. Protect your margin by selling directly to consumers or butchers, not through middlemen who take a cut. Remember, a small margin on many pigs is better than a big margin on few. Daily sales mean steady cash flow.

lessons.title: Direct to Consumer
lessons.body: Selling directly to consumersâfamilies, restaurants, and small shopsâcan earn you 20-40% more than selling to traders. Consumers pay for convenience and quality. You can sell live pigs, butchered cuts, or processed products like sausages. Start by targeting neighbors, friends, and local eateries. A restaurant might buy 2 pigs per week if you offer consistent supply and good cuts. Advertise using WhatsApp groups, Facebook Marketplace, and community notice boards. Post photos of your pigs and prices. For example, 'Fresh pork available every Friday. 1 kg = 3,500 shillings. Order before Thursday.' Offer delivery for a small fee. To sell direct, you need a reliable slaughter and cutting setup. If you don't have a slaughter slab, partner with a local butcher who charges a fee per pig (e.g., 500 shillings). You can also sell live pigs to consumers who slaughter at homeâcommon in rural areas. Price your cuts: a whole carcass might sell for 2,800 shillings per kg, but individual cuts like ribs or loin can go for 4,000-5,000 shillings per kg. That increases your margin. However, direct selling takes time. You must handle orders, slaughter, cutting, packaging, and delivery. Start small: sell to 5 regular customers. Use a cooler box with ice to keep meat fresh. For daily sales from batch farrowing, direct-to-consumer works best if you have a steady supply of pigs every week. You can also offer subscription boxes: '10 kg pork per month for 30,000 shillings.' This gives you predictable income. Keep records of each customer's preferences. Ask for feedback. Happy customers refer others. In many African cities, demand for pork is growing. Position yourself as a reliable local supplier. Avoid selling on creditâcash on delivery. If a customer wants credit, set a limit and charge a small interest. Direct selling is more work but more rewarding.

lessons.title: When to Add Value
lessons.body: Adding value means turning live pigs into products like sausages, bacon, ham, or cooked pork. It can double or triple your income, but only if you have the right conditions. First, check demand. Are there supermarkets, hotels, or delis in your area that sell processed pork? If not, you might need to create demand through sampling and promotion. Second, check regulations. In many African countries, processing meat requires a license from the health department. You need a clean facility, running water, and refrigeration. If you cannot afford a facility, start with simple value addition: sell pork cuts in smaller packages, or offer marinated ribs ready for grilling. That requires only a freezer and packaging. Third, calculate costs. A sausage-making machine costs 200,000 to 500,000 shillings. Spices and casings add 200 shillings per kg. If you sell sausages at 6,000 shillings per kg and your cost is 3,500, you make 2,500 per kg. But you must sell enough volume. Start by making 10 kg per week. Test the market. If it sells, scale up. For daily pig sales from batch farrowing, value addition helps you use lower-value cuts. Instead of selling a whole pig to a butcher at 2,500 per kg, you can turn the shoulders and bellies into sausages and sell the prime cuts fresh. That increases your overall revenue per pig by 30-50%. However, value addition takes time and labor. You might need to hire one person. Only add value when you have more pigs than you can sell live, or when live prices are low. Also consider seasonality: during festivals, demand for fresh pork is high, so sell live. During slow periods, process. Start small with one product, like sausages, and master it. Get a food handler's certificate. Keep your facility clean. Bad meat can ruin your reputation. Many successful pig farmers in Kenya, Uganda, and Nigeria started with direct sales and then added value after 2 years. Be patient.

lessons.title: A 12-Month Growth Plan
lessons.body: A 12-month growth plan helps you move from selling a few pigs to a steady daily business. Start by setting clear monthly targets. For example, Month 1-3: sell 2 pigs per week to 2 butchers. Month 4-6: increase to 4 pigs per week and add one live trader. Month 7-9: add direct-to-consumer sales, targeting 10 regular customers. Month 10-12: start value addition with sausages, selling 20 kg per week. To achieve this, you need to plan your batches. With batch farrowing, you group sows to farrow together every 4-6 weeks. That gives you a consistent number of pigs ready for sale each week. For 4 pigs per week, you need about 8 sows farrowing every 5 weeks (assuming 10 piglets weaned per sow, 90% survival, and 24 weeks to market weight). Adjust based on your performance. Keep records of farrowing dates, weaning weights, and sales. Use a simple notebook or a smartphone app like Farmbrite or PigCHAMP. Each month, review your progress. Are you meeting sales targets? If not, why? Maybe feed quality is poor, or disease. Fix problems early. Reinvest profits: 30% into feed, 20% into expanding housing, 10% into marketing, and keep 40% as savings or emergency fund. Build relationships with buyers. Invite them to see your farm. Show them your healthy pigs. That builds trust. As you grow, consider hiring one worker to help with feeding and cleaning. Pay them fairly. Also, join a pig farmers' cooperative to access cheaper feed and share transport. In Month 12, evaluate: can you sell 6 pigs per week? If yes, plan for Year 2: add a second batch farrowing group, buy a feed mixer, and maybe open a small retail outlet. Remember, growth is gradual. Don't overstock. Many farmers fail because they expand too fast without a market. Secure buyers first, then increase production. Your 12-month plan should be written down and reviewed monthly. Celebrate small wins. Daily sales mean daily cashâuse it wisely.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a butcher and a live trader?
options: A) Butchers buy live pigs, live traders buy carcasses
B) Butchers slaughter and sell meat, live traders resell live pigs
C) Butchers pay cash, live traders pay later
D) Butchers only buy from farms, live traders only buy from markets
quiz.explanation: Butchers slaughter pigs and sell meat, while live traders buy live pigs to resell.

quiz.q: Why is it important to have multiple buyers for daily pig sales?
options: B) To avoid dependence on one buyer and balance price and reliability
C) To reduce the number of pigs you sell
quiz.explanation: Having multiple buyers reduces risk if one buyer stops buying or pays poorly.

quiz.q: What is a typical weight range for pigs that butchers prefer?
quiz.explanation: Butchers usually prefer pigs weighing 80-100 kg live for good carcass yield.

quiz.q: What should be included in a contract with a butcher?
options: A) Only the price per kg
B) Number of pigs, weight range, price, payment terms, and penalties
D) The farmer's bank account number only
quiz.explanation: A good contract covers quantity, weight, price, payment, and penalties for missed deliveries.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of a written contract with a butcher?
options: A) It guarantees higher prices forever
B) It reduces disputes and helps you plan batches
C) It eliminates the need for weighing pigs
D) It allows you to sell below cost
quiz.explanation: A written contract clarifies expectations and reduces disputes, helping you plan production.

quiz.q: How long should a trial contract with a butcher last?
quiz.explanation: A 3-month trial allows both parties to assess reliability and adjust terms.

quiz.q: What is the first step in pricing to protect margin?
options: A) Ask the buyer what they will pay
B) Calculate your cost per kg of live weight
C) Set a price equal to your neighbor's
D) Sell at the highest price in the market
quiz.explanation: You must know your cost per kg to set a floor price and ensure profit.

quiz.q: Feed cost is what percentage of total pig production costs?
quiz.explanation: Feed typically accounts for 60-70% of the cost of raising a pig.

quiz.q: If a pig eats 250 kg of feed and feed costs 1,200 shillings per 50 kg bag, what is the feed cost per pig?
quiz.explanation: 250 kg / 50 kg = 5 bags; 5 x 1,200 = 6,000 shillings.

quiz.q: What should you do if a live trader offers a price below your cost?
options: A) Accept it to keep the buyer
B) Sell anyway and hope for better next time
C) Refuse and find a buyer who pays above cost
D) Reduce pig weight to lower cost
quiz.explanation: Selling below cost leads to losses; find a buyer who pays a profitable price.

quiz.q: Why is tracking every sale in a notebook important?
options: A) To show off to other farmers
B) To calculate average margin and make pricing decisions
quiz.explanation: Records help you calculate actual margins and adjust prices or costs.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of selling directly to consumers?
options: A) You can sell lower quality meat
B) You earn 20-40% more than selling to traders
C) You don't need to slaughter pigs
D) You can sell on credit easily
quiz.explanation: Direct-to-consumer sales often yield higher prices because you bypass middlemen.

quiz.q: Which tool is useful for advertising direct pork sales?
options: A) WhatsApp groups and Facebook Marketplace
quiz.explanation: Social media and messaging apps are low-cost and effective for local direct sales.

quiz.q: What is a subscription box in direct pork sales?
options: A) A box of live pigs
B) A monthly delivery of a set amount of pork for a fixed price
C) A free sample of sausages
D) A contract with a butcher
quiz.explanation: A subscription box provides predictable income by delivering regular pork orders.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid selling on credit in direct-to-consumer sales?
options: B) It reduces cash flow and increases risk of non-payment
C) Customers prefer to pay cash
quiz.explanation: Credit sales tie up your cash and can lead to losses if customers don't pay.

quiz.q: What is value addition in pig farming?
options: A) Selling live pigs at a higher price
B) Turning live pigs into processed products like sausages
C) Adding more pigs to your herd
quiz.explanation: Value addition means processing pork into products to increase revenue per pig.

quiz.q: What is a prerequisite for large-scale value addition like sausage making?
options: A) A license from health department and clean facility
quiz.explanation: Processing meat requires compliance with health regulations and a hygienic facility.

quiz.q: When is the best time to add value to your pigs?
options: A) When live prices are high
B) When you have more pigs than you can sell live or live prices are low
C) At the start of your farming business
quiz.explanation: Value addition helps use surplus pigs or when live market prices are low.

quiz.q: What is a simple value addition that requires only a freezer and packaging?
options: B) Selling marinated ribs ready for grilling
quiz.explanation: Marinated ribs are a low-investment value-added product that needs minimal equipment.

quiz.q: How much can value addition increase revenue per pig?
quiz.explanation: Value addition can raise overall revenue per pig by 30-50% by using lower-value cuts.

quiz.q: What is the first step in a 12-month growth plan?
options: B) Set clear monthly sales targets
quiz.explanation: Setting monthly targets gives direction and measurable goals.

quiz.q: In batch farrowing, how often do groups of sows farrow?
quiz.explanation: Batch farrowing groups sows to farrow every 4-6 weeks for consistent pig production.

quiz.q: To sell 4 pigs per week, approximately how many sows do you need farrowing every 5 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Assuming 10 piglets weaned per sow and 90% survival, 8 sows produce about 72 pigs per batch, enough for 4 per week over 5 weeks.

quiz.q: What percentage of profits should be reinvested into feed?
quiz.explanation: Reinvesting 30% into feed ensures you can continue feeding pigs for the next cycle.

quiz.q: Why should you secure buyers before increasing production?
options: A) To avoid overstocking and financial loss
C) To qualify for government subsidies
quiz.explanation: Without buyers, extra pigs may not sell, leading to losses from feeding costs.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of joining a pig farmers' cooperative?
options: A) Access to cheaper feed and shared transport
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives can negotiate bulk discounts on feed and share transport costs.

quiz.q: How often should you review your 12-month growth plan?
quiz.explanation: Monthly reviews help you track progress and make timely adjustments.

quiz.q: What is a common reason many pig farmers fail when expanding?
options: A) They expand too fast without a market
B) They keep too many records
C) They sell too many pigs
D) They pay workers too much
quiz.explanation: Expanding production without securing buyers leads to unsold pigs and financial losses.

quiz.q: What should you do in Month 12 of your growth plan?
options: B) Evaluate progress and plan for Year 2
quiz.explanation: Evaluating progress helps you set realistic goals for the next year.

quiz.q: Why is daily sales important for cash flow?
options: A) It provides steady income to cover daily expenses
B) It reduces the need for record-keeping
C) It allows you to sell on credit
D) It eliminates the need for a contract
quiz.explanation: Daily sales generate regular cash, which is essential for buying feed and meeting other costs.
